sections.title: Build the answer
sections.intro: You've chosen your story: you moved a team's deployments from hand-run scripts to a self-service pipeline. Now tell it. Each step is a delivery decision.

options: "First, a quick primer on what a CI/CD pipeline is…"
"Deploys took three people four hours, so we shipped monthly."
"The scripts were written in 2017, then rewritten in 2019…"
"I reported to Dana, who reported to the platform director…"
questions.explanation: Context exists to establish stakes fast. The others are the three classic mistakes: a project history lesson, unnecessary org-chart detail, and explaining tech your interviewer already knows.

questions.prompt: Roughly how should a 3-minute answer split its time?
options: ~30s Context, ~30s Actions, ~2 min Results
~90s Context, ~60s Actions, ~30s Learnings
~1 min Context, ~1 min Actions, ~1 min Results
~20s Context, ~2 min Actions, ~1 min Results + Learnings
questions.explanation: About 10% / 60% / 30%. Actions are where the scored signal lives, so they get the most time.

questions.prompt: The project had three phases. How do you keep a long story easy to follow?
options: Ask the interviewer which phase to start with
Skip the middle phase to keep it short
Preview it: "I did three things: got buy-in, built it, rolled it out."
Tell everything in strict chronological order
questions.explanation: The Table of Contents technique. It lets the listener track where you are, shows organized thinking, and gives you a way back if you're interrupted. Name each theme as a conclusion, not just a topic.

questions.prompt: Which Actions sentence carries the most signal?
options: "I prototyped it on one service to win over the skeptics."
"The pipeline was assigned to me after planning."
"We built a new pipeline and rolled it out."
"I worked on the deployment pipeline project."
questions.explanation: It's specific, it's an "I" sentence, and it shows a decision with a reason behind it. "We" erases your part, "was assigned" makes the work sound like it happened to you, and "worked on" says nothing.

questions.prompt: You've spent 40 seconds on how you tuned build caching, and the interviewer's "mm-hm"s are getting shorter. What now?
options: Back up and re-explain the caching more simply
Push through — the detail proves your expertise
Ask if they'd like the full technical breakdown
Offer it as a follow-up and move to the next action
questions.explanation: The 30-second rule: if no new action has come in 30 seconds, you're stuck on one point. In an interview, a short "mm-hm" often means "move on." Add detail only until the action is clear and credible.

questions.prompt: There's no hard metric. Which Result works best?
options: "It went really well and everyone liked it."
"I'm sure it saved the company a lot of money."
"Any engineer could deploy in 15 minutes, so we shipped weekly."
"I don't have numbers, so I'll skip the results."
questions.explanation: A before/after comparison is one of the four fallbacks, along with stakeholder feedback, time or effort saved, and what newly became possible. Never skip Results, and never make up a number.

options: "I learned that communication is really important."
"I learned that pipelines are complex systems."
"I'd bring on-call in at design time — they caught a rollback gap late."
"Honestly, I wouldn't change anything about it."
questions.explanation: It's specific, it admits a real mistake, and it's something you'd actually do differently. "Nothing to change" is a red flag, and generic lessons don't stick with anyone.

questions.prompt: They ask: "What was the hardest part?" Why should this not catch you off guard?
options: You can turn it around and ask what they think
Your Results already answered it in full
It's rare — interviewers usually skip follow-ups
It's one of four follow-ups to prepare for every story
questions.explanation: What would you do differently? What was the hardest part? How did you measure success? What happened after? Expect them for every core story, and have answers ready.

questions.prompt: Why does CARL replace STAR in this course?
options: It drops Results, since metrics are often missing
It's shorter, so stories stay under a minute
It adds Learnings, and merges Situation and Task
It puts Actions first so interviewers stay engaged
questions.explanation: STAR has no place for reflection, which is essential for senior roles, and Situation and Task blur together in practice anyway.

questions.snippet: "So this system was originally built in 2016 by a contractor, then in 2018 the team tried to migrate it, which failed because of a reorg, and then in 2020…"
options: Good — the history explains why it was hard
Too vague — it needs exact dates and names
The project history lesson — cut to the stakes
Fine, as long as it stays under two minutes
questions.explanation: Context should be the minimum needed to make your Actions make sense, about 30-45 seconds. A timeline the listener doesn't need delays the signal, and their attention drifts.

questions.prompt: Your favorite project is long, and this interviewer interrupts a lot. What helps?
options: Speak faster to fit everything in
Pick a shorter, lower-scope story instead
Ask them to hold questions until the end
Front-load the Results so the outcome lands early
questions.explanation: If deep follow-ups might keep you from reaching the end, put the outcome up front. Then the interruptions add to the story instead of cutting it off.

questions.prompt: One story, three questions: perseverance, ownership, communication. How do you reuse it?
options: Never reuse a story within the same interview
Tell it exactly the same way every time
Change the facts slightly to fit each question
Foreground a different part each time; mention the rest briefly
questions.explanation: Like different movie trailers cut from the same footage. Change what you emphasize, never the facts.

questions.prompt: Your interviewer is a hiring manager who doesn't write code. How do you adjust?
options: Skip the technical parts entirely
Stay at the decisions and trade-offs level
Explain every technical term from scratch
Go deeper on the technical details to impress
questions.explanation: Match the detail to the listener. Go deeper with a peer engineer; with a manager, stay at the level of decisions and their consequences. You keep the substance, just at a different altitude.

questions.snippet:
A: "I debugged the issue."
B: "I added distributed tracing and found the Redis pool was exhausted at peak."
options: Equal — both describe the same action
A — B is too technical for an interview
A — it's concise and keeps the story moving
B — the specificity is itself evidence of skill
questions.explanation: Specific actions show how you work, so the interviewer can see you'd do it again. Vague ones could describe anybody.
